#10069. Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

In this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:

Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The new material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a big part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

This project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

In that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:

I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I launched the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

Disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

The library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

His blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a big pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

The gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

The pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

The tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

No human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

If we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

With that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were launched for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:

The three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

The pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

This is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, shows almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

What the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

One more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

The paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste says the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

To choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

Since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

Failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs launched with it have been running clean since.

The reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

The rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

And underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:

The rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

The per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

The method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

#10067. Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Threat actors don't need to rely on malware to breach organizations anymore. They're simply calling help desks and politely asking for access, with a little help from artificial intelligence.

After a disruptive cyberattack hits, customer trust can take a while to rebuild. But now threat actors are impersonating trusted brand names and existing customer accounts to abuse customer relations.

"Trust has become easier to exploit and harder to establish," a new TransUnion report warns. Threat actors use social engineering, deepfake technology, text spoofing, compromised credentials, and artificial intelligence (AI) to become whoever they need to be, whether that's a new or existing customer or the organization itself.

In light of more attacks, many organizations have improved security during sign-up and onboarding processes. Organizations must continue to adapt since "most fraud now occurs after the customer relationship has already been established," the report states. It found 58% of organizations were very or extremely concerned that fraud is evolving faster than their abilities to detect or prevent it.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The use of synthetic identities plays a big role. Threat actors can spin them up with ease, given widespread data breaches that exposed millions of individuals' sensitive information, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Scammers will replicate leaked documents or use deepfakes to bypass identity proofing checks at onboarding.

The credit reporting agency found that account login accounted for 53% of all suspected digital fraud during the first half of 2026. Conducting scams has become easier for threat actors as tooling advances, Killeen adds. Threat actors aren't just automating account creation with scripts; they're actually building logic into automated pipelines to reverse-engineer security controls, he says. That allows them to pinpoint exactly where and how defenses are blocking their attacks.

"Trust is under pressure," Killeen tells Dark Reading.

Last year the FBI warned of an uptick in cybercriminals targeting employee self-service portals — websites used for payroll, benefits, and other human resources services — at both private companies and government agencies. Threat actors created fake search engine advertisements to lure users into visiting malicious sites that mimicked legitimate companies' logos and layouts. Once the victim logged in, attackers stole login credentials and financial information.

And the situation continues to evolve. Over the past year, AI has helped criminals personalize attacks and spread them across channels — from email to Teams. Deepfakes add another layer of credibility, says Javvad Malik, lead chief information security officer (CISO) adviser at KnowBe4.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Amid booming AI adoption that security has trouble matching, the security awareness company is also seeing more attempts to exploit AI systems or take advantage of poorly configured AI tools and agents, he adds.

"The social engineering techniques remain similar, but attackers are also using AI to find weaknesses and are beginning to target AI agents directly," Malik tells Dark Reading.

The AI attack surface is ripe for the taking. New research from Check Point on brand impersonation trends from Q3 flagged a phishing campaign where threat actors impersonated Anthropic's Claude assistant. Fraudulent emails, playing up urgency with a due payment notice, requested 500 euros with an "update payment" link intended to trick users into clicking, putting their credentials and financial information at risk. Since April, KnowBe4 tracked a 228% increase in AI brand impersonation, says James Dyer, head of threat intelligence. Attackers are abusing the global focus on using AI within businesses as a perfect covert operation for their phishing attacks, he adds, warning that the problem compounds when attackers center their attacks around breaking news headlines.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

When it comes to attacks against customer relations, attackers' methods have evolved from deploying malware to exploiting identity because there's no need to write a script when they can just get a password reset, says Dave Lewis, global advisory CISO at 1Password.

The industry spent a decade training people not to click links, and attackers responded by simply asking nicely, he adds. The most common attacks he has observed don't involve "anyone in a hoodie typing furiously" but instead phoning the help desk to manipulate users into giving away multifactor authentication (MFA) codes.

"[It's] the most effective zero-day of 2026," Lewis says.

Walking in through the customer relationship management (CRM) system's front door is another tactic he has seen, pointing to the data-theft campaign against Salesforce customers that started in 2025 and continued into 2026.

"Nobody 'hacks' the CRM," Lewis tells Dark Reading. "They just log in with a key you handed to a vendor or a guest account nobody remembers creating."

The target moved from the data center to the software-as-a-service layer, where one compromised integration gives attackers many targets per compromise. Detection lags because SaaS platforms log differently from traditional infrastructure, Lewis adds.

Threat actors also use AI to build voice deepfakes from executives' public recordings, deploy them in high-pressure desk calls, and then use AI again to move through hybrid environments within minutes of gaining access. But that doesn't exactly signal an increase in sophistication, Lewis says.

"Technical sophistication is down," he says. "Operational sophistication — research, patience, scripting, follow-through — is up. It's less of the 'evil genius' and more 'well-run call center with bad intentions.'"

"What once looked legitimate and trusted can change" as threat actors slip further under the radar, cloaked behind more convincing and personalized impersonation tactics. Killeen stresses. Organizations across industries are seeing more scams, authorized fraud, and good customers being manipulated, he says.

Organizations must learn and adapt quickly because attackers aren't wasting any time. Killeen recommends that organizations take a look at their existing controls to uncover vulnerable points and understand where the biggest losses are. Even if organizations stand up strong security at the front door, they could still fall victim to downstream risks.

"It's taking a risk-based approach, looking at things holistically, and how you prioritize those things accordingly, based on your vulnerabilities," Killeen advises.

Killeen and Lewis agree that attacks against customer relations warrants checking every door leading into the CRM. That includes every OAuth application, integration, guest or portal user, and API key.

"Revoke anything without a named owner," Lewis says. "Scope the rest. Repeat quarterly because they grow back."

He also recommends that organizations fix the help desk process attackers continually abuse, rather than people who work it. Scripted identity verification for resets, callback to a number of record, and manager approval for any privileged or MFA reset are ways to reduce risk in that area.

"Drop speed metrics, like average handle time, for identity-sensitive support interactions," Lewis adds. “They drive agents to prioritize speed over verification.”

Holding less customer data is another area organizations can prioritize to limit risks. Implement retention limits on customer records, purge dormant accounts, and don't include production customer data in sandboxes, Lewis recommends.

"Data you don't hold can't be stolen," he says.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#10065. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#10064. 10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

This Cybersecurity Awareness Month's theme, "Securing the Next 250," asks us to look beyond vulnerabilities and consider what will make our digital systems resilient for generations.

When I testified before Congress with my L0pht colleagues in 1998, we warned that insecure software could put the systems society depended on at risk. Technology has changed dramatically since then, but the fundamental security questions remain familiar. Where does untrusted data enter? What authority does a component have? Who owns the risk, and how do we know a control worked?

We cannot predict the technology stack of 2276, but we can establish practices that make software trustworthy as technology evolves. These 10 are a good place to start.

Make security part of the architecture. Secure by design should describe how a system is engineered, beginning with secure defaults, approved patterns, clear trust boundaries, and controls that make insecure outcomes difficult. When security is introduced near the end of development, it must work against decisions already embedded in the architecture, while built-in controls become part of how the system operates and evolves.

Maintain an accurate picture of what you have. Every organization needs a continuously updated inventory of its applications, open source dependencies, development tools, AI models, and external services, along with clear ownership for critical systems. When a serious vulnerability emerges, teams should be able to determine quickly where the affected component is running, what it can reach, and who is responsible for addressing it.

Verify every line of code. Code should earn trust whether it was written by an employee, generated by an AI assistant, or obtained from a third party. Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that operates at the same speed as development and verifies code before it reaches production.

Make the secure path the easiest path. Developers work under constant pressure to ship, so security controls that produce excessive noise, delay builds, or pull people away from their normal tools will eventually be bypassed. Organizations should put precise feedback, approved components, and validated fixes directly into repositories, pipelines, and coding workflows, making the secure approach the most efficient way to complete the work.

Match security speed to development speed. AI is turning software insecurity into a throughput problem because teams can now produce and change code faster than manual review can follow. Testing, policy enforcement, and remediation therefore need to operate continuously across the development life cycle, with automation handling repeatable work and people concentrating on the complex decisions that require business context and judgment.

Control what enters the software supply chain. Modern applications are assembled from large volumes of code that organizations did not write, and each dependency introduces another relationship that must be understood and maintained. Teams should evaluate components when they enter a build, record their provenance, detect malicious or abandoned packages, and plan for safe upgrades, since an inventory alone cannot prevent risky software from being introduced.

Pay down security debt before it comes due. Veracode's research found that security debt now affects 82% of organizations, leaving an expanding reservoir of vulnerabilities that have remained unresolved for more than a year. As AI-powered discovery compresses years of vulnerability research into months, leaders need to fund remediation as an ongoing engineering function, define expectations for addressing the highest-risk flaws, and track whether new risk is accumulating faster than teams can remove it.

Measure the risk you remove. Most security programs can report how many vulnerabilities they found and closed, yet those activity measures do not show whether the organization has become safer. More useful measures include how long critical, exploitable flaws remain exposed, whether fix capacity is keeping pace with incoming risk and how quickly teams can reduce exposure in applications tied to sensitive data or essential business operations.

Threat-model the entire AI system. An AI agent includes far more than the model because its identity, permissions, tools, memory, data, runtime, and network access all contribute to what it can ultimately do. Organizations should authorize sensitive actions where they occur, constrain what compromised components can reach, include the runtime in data-flow analysis, and retain enough evidence to determine what the agent did when something goes wrong.

Preserve human accountability. Every important application and accepted risk needs an accountable owner, supported by evidence of the controls applied, tests performed, and decisions made throughout the software life cycle. As machines assume a larger role in writing and modifying code, people must retain enough understanding to challenge the output, recognize unexpected behavior, and demonstrate that reasonable precautions were taken.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

The next 250 years will bring technologies that we cannot name today, although the systems built with them will still have inputs, privileges, dependencies, and consequences. Lasting security will come from disciplined engineering, continuous verification, and clear responsibility, supported by people who understand how complex systems fail and know how to question the assumptions behind them.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

That hacker mindset has served the industry well, and we need to keep teaching it to developers, defenders, and the next generation of security researchers. The tools and architectures will continue to change, while our responsibility to build systems worthy of trust will endure.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Founder and Chief Security Evangelist, Veracode

Chris Wysopal is the Chief Security Evangelist at Veracode, responsible for enhancing the company’s industry presence, advocating robust security practices, and fostering customer and peer relationships. Prior to co-founding Veracode in 2006, Chris was vice president of research and development at security consultancy @stake, which was acquired by Symantec. In the 1990s, Chris was one of the original vulnerability researchers at The L0pht, a hacker think tank, where he was one of the first to publicize the risks of insecure software. He has testified to the US Congress on the subjects of government security and how vulnerabilities are discovered in software.

#10062. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

#10061. 'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

An ongoing supply chain attack is harvesting credentials and sensitive data from thousands of developer repositories.

An ongoing attack is abusing compromised GitHub tokens to harvest cloud secrets and credentials from thousands of developer repositories, bringing into focus how compromised developer accounts can provide a gateway into enterprise cloud environments.

Dubbed "Gheist," the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches — or versions of a project's code — across more than 850 compromised GitHub accounts, according to a report published over the weekend by Wiz Research.

The campaign affects everything from personal projects to private enterprise repositories, although public repositories are protected by safeguards GitHub introduced in July, according to the report.

"The control GitHub added is focused on protecting public repositories from workflow abuse vectors," Wiz researcher Rami McCarthy tells Dark Reading. However, "once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply," he adds.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

Wiz also found overlap between Gheist-affected GitHub accounts and other abuse campaigns, including repository-based malware distribution, attempts to exploit GitHub Actions for computing resources, and possible infections linked to other malware operations.

This overlap — which distinguishes Gheist from similar campaigns — suggests stolen developer tokens may be reused or shared among threat actors, "demonstrating the complexity and activity of this threat landscape," McCarthy says.

The campaign relies on a workflow named "sync-check," which is committed to each repository accessible through a stolen token, the researchers wrote.

"The workflow seeks to print the repository’s secrets into its own workflow log," they wrote. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent 'gheist,' which gives the campaign its name."

Wiz began tracking the activity Sept. 15 and said the operation remains active and evolving as of Oct. 24. The researchers reported the activity to GitHub, and about two-thirds of the implicated accounts are no longer available, which "likely indicates response activity," according to the report.

The tokens appear to have come primarily from two sources: infostealer malware and credentials exposed in earlier software supply chain compromises, the researchers noted.

GitHub tokens authorize users and applications to access repositories, code, and administrative functions, making them valuable to attackers seeking to compromise projects and organizations.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to create branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters. The attackers then add the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, using the commit message "ci: sync config," according to the report.

"The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner," the researchers wrote. The resulting push event triggers a workflow that attempts to print environment variables and repository secrets into its log. The attack encodes the output using Base32 before retrieving the logs through the GitHub API and deleting the workflow run seconds later.

"Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block," the researchers explained.

A key finding is that Wiz observed successful attacks in private repositories and enterprise environments, where the public-repository safeguard did not apply. Most GitHub-targeted activity, by contrast, primarily affects public repositories, McCarthy tells Dark Reading.

"The attack succeeded in the environments organizations considered safest because a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority," says James Matchett, head of security at supply chain security firm Cloudsmith, in an email interview. "'Private' is not a control. Scoped, short-lived credentials, a tight inventory of what can push and pull, and the discipline to rotate after every incident are the control.”

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Wiz observed the attackers cycling through tokens belonging to multiple users and automation accounts, and cloning private repositories before planting malicious workflows. Within hours, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager, the researchers added.

Wiz estimates that the campaign affected "on the scale of a dozen companies," McCarthy says. However, "we have not seen consistent or automated abuse outside of mass cloning of GitHub repositories and the core credential theft," he says.

Token abuse is an increasingly common way for attackers to infiltrate organizations through the developer pipeline. Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors exploiting GitHub flaws. Defenders therefore must treat developer projects as critical organizational assets.

To defend against Gheist and other forms of token abuse, Wiz urged security teams to hunt for malicious GitHub Actions workflows, rotate exposed secrets, and treat compromised self-hosted runners as potential infrastructure breaches.

More specifically, defenders should look for branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message "ci: sync config," the researchers advised. Administrators also should review GitHub audit logs for workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion, as well as activity from the user agent "gheist."

For broader protection against GitHub token abuse, Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at security firm Secure.com, recommends that organizations "replace long-lived personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens" and "require reviewers on any environment that holds production secrets." These measures can help limit attackers' ability to access sensitive credentials even if they obtain valid tokens.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#10059. The Port That Does Not Exist

Port 0 is the port you are not supposed to use, so nobody looks there. So we put an IRC network on it. Then I got curious whether anyone else had, and scanned all of IPv4 for port 0. Turns out we weren't alone, and some of our neighbours really shouldn't be there.

Ask any program to listen on port 0 and it will hand you a socket on port 47193...or 58037...or whatever the kernel felt like that day. Port 0 is not a port you can have. It is the number you pass when you want the operating system to pick one for you.

But a TCP header is just bytes. The destination port field is 16 bits wide, and 0x0000 fits in 16 bits as well as anything else does. Nothing on the wire stops a packet from being addressed to port 0. Your tools will refuse it, your browser will block it, and your scanner's default port list skips it, because everyone agrees it isn't a real port.

Which makes it a pretty good place to hide things, whether anyone meant to or not. So we did some TCP cowboy shit & port scanned the entire fucking internet for open ports on port 0, which uncovered some interesting unexpected findings.

The standards are thin on this. RFC 9293, the 2022 consolidation of the TCP spec, defines the source and destination port as "16 bits" and leaves it there. It has no rule against zero.

IANA lists 0/tcp and 0/udp as Reserved, pointing at RFC 6335. That RFC splits the port space into System (0–1023), User (1024–49151) and Dynamic (49152–65535) ranges, and explains what "Reserved" means:

So port 0 is not forbidden. It is set aside. The only place zero has a defined protocol meaning is UDP: RFC 768 makes the source port optional, and "if not used, a value of zero is inserted." TCP has nothing like that.

Port 0's reputation comes from the sockets API, not the wire. When you call bind() with sin_port = 0, you are not asking for port 0. You are asking for any port. The ip(7) man page lists every case where Linux hands out an ephemeral port: bind() with port 0, listen() on an unbound socket, connect() on an unbound socket, and sendto() on an unbound datagram socket.

The range comes from net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, which defaults to 32768 60999 on Linux, not the 49152–65535 that IANA calls Dynamic. And asking for port 0 needs no privileges. __inet_bind() only checks CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE when the requested port is non-zero.

How the kernel picks is more interesting than I expected. In net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c (v6.8), inet_csk_find_open_port() starts at a random offset and then does this:

It walks the range in steps of two. The function above it says it outright: "We try to allocate an odd port (and leave even ports for connect())." Outgoing connections go through __inet_hash_connect() in inet_hashtables.c, which implements RFC 6056 Algorithm 4 (double-hash port selection) and takes the even ports first. The kernel splits the range by parity so servers asking for "any port" and clients making outbound connections don't fight over the same numbers. If SO_REUSEADDR is set, bind() also tries the lower half of the range before the upper half.

That is easy to test. On a stock Ubuntu box running Linux 6.8:

So when your program says "listen on port 0", the kernel hears "give me an odd number between 32768 and 61000." No normal program can listen on port 0.

You can bypass all of this with raw sockets, but if you just want to cheat, you can simply forward the port to another with iptables/nftables. As a fun proof of concept, I set up my IRC network at irc.supernets.org to accept plaintext connections on port 0 and SSL connections on port 1. JUST TO FLEX. ð

A SYN arrives for port 0, netfilter rewrites the destination to 6667 where the ircd is actually listening, and the reply is rewritten back on the way out. The ircd never knows. Port 1 does the same for TLS on 6697.

Getting a server onto port 0 was the easy part. Getting a client there is where tools give up. I pointed everything I had at our own server on port 0:

That last one is strange, because the TCP connection underneath it is fine. The problem is that the kernel says it isn't, and it does that on purpose. Here is inet_getname() in net/ipv4/af_inet.c, which backs getpeername():

Linux uses "destination port is 0" as its internal marker for "this socket isn't connected to anything." A socket that really is connected to port 0 trips that check, so getpeername() returns ENOTCONN on a working connection.

Python's ssl.wrap_socket() calls getpeername() to decide whether the socket is connected, gets ENOTCONN, decides it isn't, switches to non-blocking and tries a recv(1), gets EAGAIN, and raises BlockingIOError. The TCP connection is fine. It just reports that it doesn't exist. Python's asyncio does TLS through memory buffers instead of wrap_socket(), never asks, and works.

You can't scan port 0 with connect()-based tools for all the reasons above, but masscan doesn't use the kernel's TCP stack. It builds its own SYN packets, so port 0 is just another number.

1,173,626 addresses answered with a SYN-ACK.

That sounds like a lot of people using port 0. It isn't. Grouped by /24, the responses are packed into a few thousand dense blocks:

8% of those /24s hold 78% of the responding IPs. Whole blocks answer on every address: 172.65.0.0/16 returned 65,534 of 65,536. That isn't 65,534 servers. It's a firewall or router at the edge answering the SYN for everything behind it. 1,116,675 addresses completed the handshake and never sent a single byte.

56,951 addresses did send something. Almost all of it looked like this:

F5 BIG-IP load balancers write the reason for a reset into the RST packet, and masscan saved it as a banner. That's 53,741 of the 56,951 (94%), and 46,583 of them are in 132.246.0.0/16 alone. Drop those, plus 305 hosts returning the same fixed (Ref.Id: ?...?) token, and 2,905 addresses are left. That's about 0.25% of everything that answered.

Nobody is running anything exotic on port 0. It's the same stuff that's on every other port: SSH, databases, telnet, FTP. What stands out is how much of it is embedded gear. dropbear, micro_httpd, NAS certificates from QNAP, Synology and Buffalo, DVRs, power switches. Some of it clearly comes from one device model rolled out across an ISP:

My guess is that nobody at those ISPs picked port 0 on purpose: a port-forward or NAT rule shipped in a CPE config with the external port left at zero, and the device honored it. Then there are the hosting providers. GigaCloud (Ukraine), VDCBY (Belarus) and SiS Distribution (Thailand) have SSH on port 0 with 18, 13 and 10 different SSH version strings. Different builds means different machines, so these are individual customers, not one firmware image.

GigaCloud also accounts for 16 of the 80 mail servers on port 0, mostly Ukrainian organisations: mail.dtek-kem.com.ua (DTEK, the Ukrainian energy company), smtp01.health24.ua, mx.eastenergy.com.ua, mail.citrus.com.ua, and two government servers, mail.depfin.dn.gov.ua and mail.sed-rada.gov.ua. Why they all share this setup, I don't know. Elsewhere in mail: a Uruguayan government host, prod-carbonium01.rionegro.gub.uy, and mssante.elsan.care (62.106.147.123), a submission server for MSSantÃ©, the French national secure health messaging system, run by the private hospital group Elsan. When masscan poked it, it replied:

The rest of the router logins look the same as they would on port 80. A D-Link DSL-2740B (37.103.36.12 and two others), with "admin" already filled in as the username: two in French at Orange and Nerim in France, one in English at Wind Tre in Italy. A Linksys "Router Access" page in El Salvador (200.31.162.80). A plain "Sign in" form titled "Router Admin" on seven cloud servers: four at Hetzner, two at Online SAS, one at DigitalOcean.

One didn't bother with a login at all. A 3G/4G "Wireless Mobile Router" on China Unicom (183.93.33.155) serves its full status page on port 0 to anyone who asks: its WAN IP, LAN, WAN and wireless MAC addresses, SSID, firmware build, uptime, memory usage and whether DHCP is on.

Browsers won't open a URL with :0 in it, so to see the web interfaces I ran a small relay: listen on a local port, connect out to the target on port 0, pipe the bytes through, and point headless Chromium at the local port. 160 addresses speak HTTP on port 0, and 85 rendered a page.

A Gira HomeServer 4 (46.186.48.86), a KNX home and building automation controller, with its start page, debug page and monitor links sitting on port 0.

A Trane Tracer Synchrony login (201.171.202.25), which is HVAC and building control.

The web pages were the easy part to read. The more interesting devices don't speak HTTP. They send binary the moment you connect, and figuring out what they are meant matching bytes against nmap's probe database, Wireshark dissectors and, in one case, a disassembled vendor client.

A Beckhoff PLC with its screen open to anyone. 46.178.29.102, on Proximus in Belgium, sends this on connect:

The CX5120 is a Beckhoff embedded PC running Windows CE, the kind that runs TwinCAT and drives a machine. The protocol is CERDISP, Windows CE Remote Display, which Beckhoff's own security guideline lists as open on TCP 987 by default. I disassembled Beckhoff's client, CERHOST.exe 2.0.4.0. It reads a 0x130-byte info block first, which is the 30 01 00 00 at the start of the banner. Then it checks a magic word: 0x6a6d6d05 means no password, 0x6a6d6d06 means password required. This one sends 05 6d 6d 6a. Then a 1366×768 resolution (56 05, 00 03) and screen update data. CERHOST also sends mouse and keyboard input. So this is a PLC's screen that anyone can watch and operate, with no password, on port 0.

An Omron PLC that was too busy to talk. 194.49.59.232 (AireNetworks, Spain) answered with an Omron FINS/TCP frame:

Command 1 is the server's Node Address Data Send, and error code 0x20 is "All connections are in use." It is a FINS endpoint, the protocol used to read and write Omron PLC memory, and it turned us away only because its connection slots were full. Five days later it said the same thing. A second host, 14.49.206.64 (KT, Korea), repeats an Omron Host Link frame, @FFF07F000000018C3D*, over and over. The XOR of everything before 3D is 0x3D, so the checksum is valid, but unit FF is outside the normal 00–31 range. The framing is Omron. The device behind it I couldn't pin down.

A Modbus master. 155.93.146.109 (South Africa) doesn't wait to be polled. It polls you: 10 04 00 00 00 02 72 8a is slave 16, Read Input Registers 0–1, with a valid CRC-16/MODBUS. Something out there is a SCADA master on port 0 asking whoever connects for two registers. Another host, 85.198.27.114 (Iran), repeats a 7e-framed 7-byte payload with a valid Modbus CRC, which looks like a serial-to-TCP bridge.

A power quality meter. 166.169.193.134 on Verizon Wireless answers telnet with SEL-735 Telnet Server. The SEL-735 is a Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories revenue and power quality meter, the kind utilities put on substations and feeders. This one is on a cellular modem.

Factory telemetry. 175.202.128.103 (KT, Korea) sends an HTTP POST at whoever connects:

kq-china.net is Zhejiang Keqiang Intelligent Control, which makes monitoring systems for injection moulding machines. uIP is Adam Dunkels' tiny embedded TCP/IP stack. A collector on a factory floor is pushing per-machine status to whoever connects, and masscan, confused, filed it as Minecraft.

A Swedish alarm. 82.183.26.214 (Telenor, Sweden) sends an STX/ETX frame containing "Kommunikationslarm medelvÃ¤rde", Swedish for "communication alarm, mean value." I don't know the device.

Burglar alarm communicators. Five hosts, three in Mexico and two in Spain, send a greeting of about 56 bytes, with a 2-byte length prefix up front. That matches the README of DSC-TLink, a reverse-engineered client for DSC's alarm communicators: "opening a TCP connection with the TL280 on port 3062. The TL280 will immediately send a packet of 56 bytes." The TL280 family is the IP/cellular communicator on DSC PowerSeries Neo alarm panels, and this is the DLS path used to program and monitor the panel. Here's 213.181.95.33:

(The 0a before the ICCID came out of the scan as 20, because our banner storage squashed whitespace bytes into spaces. I put it back.) The CRC-16 over the 42 bytes starting at 05 05 05 00 27 (polynomial 0xD003, from DSC-TLink's DLSProNetHeader.cs) comes out 0xea79, which is the ea 79 that follows. The MAC starts 00:03:4F, the IEEE OUI for Sur-Gard Security, DSC's receiver brand. And the device ID field on the cellular models is the SIM card's ICCID:

All three ICCIDs pass the Luhn check, and their prefixes say where the SIMs are from: 89 34 is Spain, 89 52 is Mexico. According to DSC-TLink, the AES key for the rest of the session is built from data in this greeting.

Alarm communicators that tell you the password. Three Spanish hosts, 109.167.87.236, 85.87.152.80 and 88.3.213.39, run telnet on an Alwon E20, a Notifier/Honeywell IP/GPRS alarm communicator module:

Notifier's manual agrees: telnet password, "1234 por defecto." I didn't try it.

Time clocks. 187.235.160.47 and one other host at UNINET in Mexico repeat a5 00 00 00 00 7f 00 00 e0 5c. That's an Anviz time-and-attendance frame: a5, a 4-byte device ID of 0, command 7f, zero length, and a CRC-16/MCRF4XX of 0x5ce0 sent low byte first. Open-source Anviz SDKs call 0x7f a ping.

Home automation. Five hosts answer *#*1##, the OpenWebNet ACK used by BTicino and Legrand home automation gateways: 190.113.106.159 (Costa Rica), 171.242.179.164 (Vietnam), 187.145.124.63 (Mexico), 105.157.199.125 (Morocco) and 213.7.222.134 (Cyprus). 219.241.160.119 in Korea is a SiHAS HCM-300 Ver 2.12 > prompt, a Shina System smart heating thermostat. And 192.119.63.143 (wilhelm.tel, Germany) is a mediola a.i.o. Gateway that sends its encrypted cloud request to whoever connects: POST /ra/d HTTP/1.1 host: mediola-ws.elasticbeanstalk.com.

A debug menu. Three hosts on SK Telecom in Korea, 42.42.150.116, 42.42.203.12 and 42.42.201.80, greet you with this:

192.168.225.x is the default subnet on Qualcomm LTE modules like the Quectel EC2x, so it's probably a cellular IoT device. Which product, I don't know.

A power strip. 64.201.180.254 (Gatewest, Canada) runs a Remote Power Controller v1.41i that prints its whole outlet table, circuit, name, status and boot delay, before asking for a login. Others ask only for a password but label themselves first: MGTN CO - Right Rack - Bottom, Power Switch, 151 Front Street.

SAProuters leaking their build. Four hosts are SAProuter, the SAP gateway that relays connections into SAP systems. They accepted the connection, waited 5 seconds for a route request that never came, and then sent back an NI_RTERR error packet with a lot of detail:

Every one gives away the SAProuter version (40.4), the SAP kernel release, the router's hostname, the server's local clock, and whether it's a Windows build (D:/) or not.

RustDesk. Four hosts, 93.118.140.111, 78.38.90.162 (Iran), 39.48.42.201 and 103.213.111.82 (Pakistan), open with HJ. That isn't a magic string. In RustDesk's bytes_codec.rs, the low two bits of the first byte give the header size and the rest gives the length, so 0x48 means an 18-byte message follows. 0x4a is protobuf field 9, Hash, which carries a salt and a challenge:

The salt stays the same per host. The challenge is six random characters, new on every connection. That's the password challenge a RustDesk client answers before it gets the desktop. 103.213.111.82 sends a 32-character salt, which is what newer versions use.

Winflector. Eight hosts run Winflector, a Polish remote application server. 193.32.180.51 sends Terminal client version too old - please update to version 4.0.0.1 and then an RSA public key in DER form, with exponent 17, which is Crypto++'s default. The versions are sent byte-reversed: 04 03 00 04 is 4.0.3.4. All six versions I saw are on Winflector's own version list. The hosts are in Cape Verde (156.238.40.243, 156.238.47.54 and one more), Malaysia (202.187.2.203 and one more), Poland (193.32.180.51), Ghana (80.87.66.51) and India (49.204.146.227).

VNC with no password. Of the 39 VNC servers, one doesn't ask for anything. 107.174.67.223 answers with security type none and a desktop name of resolv.moe, meow meow meow :3 haiiii!!, and an 850×591 framebuffer. Four more just send RFB 005.000.

Phone switches. 117.236.74.58 (BSNL, India) is Asterisk Call Manager/2.10.5, the Asterisk Manager Interface from Asterisk 13.26–13.34. Once logged in, AMI can originate calls and run console commands. 38.229.159.25 (France) and 41.60.171.20 (Liquid) send 04 00 fb ff LAPK, the 3CX tunnel protocol.

Cameras and NAS. exacqVision video surveillance servers on 8 hosts, including two at OneCleveland (204.156.216.130 and 204.156.198.238), send a 56-byte header ending in three values that change on every connection. Six QNAP NAS boxes expose RTRR (Realtime Remote Replication, ab ca a5 5d ...), on 202.184.138.61 in Malaysia and five others in Austria, Sri Lanka, Spain and Italy. Two Rifatron DVRs send RIFA, 42.200.149.78 in Hong Kong and 14.241.231.170 in Vietnam. One more is a UMS WebViewer DVR stream in Japan (123.242.213.10).

The rest of the RPC zoo. 223.76.20.55 (China Mobile) is ZeroC Ice, IceP 1.0 Validate Connection. 191.13.74.178 (Telefonica, Brazil) sends just ac ed 00 05, the header of a Java serialization stream, and then nothing else. 119.152.239.20 (Pakistan) sends a bare HTTP/2 SETTINGS frame with the same bytes as a default grpc-go server. 212.80.175.132 (Spain) has things backwards and sends us a full TLS 1.2 ClientHello. And 116.75.83.213 (Hathway, India) responds with RP-Version: 5.0 and RP-Application-Reason: 80108bff, which is Sony PlayStation Remote Play, most likely a PS4.

21 addresses don't wait to be asked. Connect to port 0 and they start streaming comma-separated text, about 7.5 KB of it per host in our capture:

That's SMDR (Station Message Detail Recording) output from an Avaya IP Office phone system. The fields line up with Avaya's documented layout: call start, connected time, ring time, caller, direction, called and dialled number, a call ID that starts at 1,000,000, then the two parties as E for extension or T for trunk, with names like "Line 31.1". Each host handed over 37 to 62 calls with real phone numbers, staff names, extension numbers and internal addresses. The oldest record is from December 2018. The newest is from a few days before the scan. Several hosts start with records that are years old, which I can't explain: 94.30.72.110 opened with calls from 2018-12-21, 31.10.39.182 with 2023-09-18.

Nothing was sent to get this. IP Office pushes SMDR records to whatever connects to its SMDR port, and on these 21 hosts that port is reachable on port 0. masscan stops reading at about 7.5 KB, so that's only the first few dozen calls per host.

19 of the 21 are in the UK, on BT, Wavenet, Gamma, TalkTalk, Plusnet and a handful of smaller business ISPs. One is in the US and one in South Africa. However these ended up on port 0, anyone who connects can read the company's call history.

Come say hi on the port that doesn't exist. If your client lets you.

Connect to SuperNETs on port 0 (plaintext) or port 1 (TLS) at irc.supernets.org, or reach out at acid.vegas@acid.vegas. We hang out in #war.
